question: Do groups with more of the exposure have more of the outcome?

morgenstern1995.cite: Morgenstern (1995). Ecologic studies in epidemiology: concepts, principles, and methods. Annual Review of Public Health 16.
morgenstern1995.checked: only the abstract could be read, on the Annual Reviews article page (in Chrome, 20 Nov 2026); the full text is a PDF that was not opened, so every quote is from the abstract; the volume is from the DOI and the page range was not read

steps.title: Pick groups
steps.text: The units of the study are groups such as countries, regions or years, not the people in them.

quotes.text: An ecologic study focuses on the comparison of groups, rather than individuals

steps.title: Use group numbers
steps.text: Each group gets one number per variable: an average or rate summarised from its members, a feature of its environment, or a property only a group can have, such as a law.

quotes.text: Variables in an ecologic analysis may be aggregate measures, environmental measures, or global measures.

steps.title: By place or time
steps.text: Compare groups side by side in one period, follow one population's rates over time, or do both.

quotes.text: whether subjects grouped by place (multiple-group study), by time (time-trend study), or place and time (mixed study)

steps.title: Relate the rates
steps.text: Plot or regress the groups' outcome rates on their exposure levels. Be clear whether the claim is about groups or about the people in them.

quotes.text: The purpose of an ecologic analysis may be to make biologic inferences about effects on individual risks or to make ecologic inferences about effects on group rates.

steps.title: Mind the leap
steps.text: Group data do not show which people within a group were exposed and also fell ill, so a pattern across groups need not hold for individuals.

quotes.text: individual-level data are missing on the joint distribution, of variables within groups
there are many methodologic problems that severely limit causal inference, including ecologic and cross-level bias

exercise.title: Regions or people?
exercise.intro: Five regions, each a circle at its average exposure and average outcome. Look at the regions first, then show the people inside them.
exercise.data_label: Example data, made up for this exercise; the same seed draws the same people on every visit.
